episode.throughLine: A pupil who arrived unable to read learned amid ridicule and support, then addressed her graduating class without knowing what work would follow.

facts.statement: Anne Sullivan entered Perkins on October 7, 1880, aged fourteen after years at Tewksbury Almshouse, unable to read or write her name.

sourceRefs.locator: Early challenges, Tewksbury paragraphs; Life-changing moment, final arrival sentence and next paragraph.

facts.statement: Institutional accounts describe ridicule over Sullivan's lack of schooling and spelling, with humiliation, anger, and shame.

sourceRefs.locator: Life-changing moment, peer ridicule; Perkins experience, first paragraph.

facts.statement: Sullivan learned to read and advanced in her studies; she recalled learning quickly.

sourceRefs.locator: Quoted recollection beginning The years at Tewksbury.

facts.statement: Sullivan later recalled a weekly Shakespeare class as especially absorbing and remembered the lasting importance of poetry.

sourceRefs.locator: Quoted recollection beginning She [the teacher] had a regular class.

facts.statement: Some staff helped Sullivan; she formed a close relationship with house mother Sophia Hopkins, and improved vision enabled print reading.

sourceRefs.locator: Perkins experience, paragraph beginning After the first two years.

facts.statement: The school account reports rule-breaking and threatened expulsion, with staff interventions.

sourceRefs.locator: Perkins experience, paragraph beginning Sullivan learned to excel.

facts.statement: Sullivan delivered her valedictory address on June 1, 1886, aged twenty.
In her address Sullivan thanked the school's supporters and staff, acknowledged friendships, and described education continuing beyond school.

sourceRefs.locator: Opening paragraph; The search for knowledge paragraph; gratitude and Schoolmates paragraphs.

facts.statement: The school's historical account says her prospects after graduation were unclear and she feared returning to the almshouse.

sourceRefs.locator: Perkins experience, paragraph beginning Just what her especial part would be.

facts.statement: Anne Sullivan later became Helen Keller's teacher.

sourceRefs.locator: Opportunity of a lifetime and Entering Helen's world.

arc.canonicalText: She entered a school for blind children at fourteen, after years in an almshouse. She could not yet read or write her name. She was beginning school.
arc.sourceNote: Source-led vignette, not recreated scenes. The 1886 speech is a contemporary document; school feelings and disciplinary history are retrospective accounts. No full-moment or publication approval is asserted.

arc.canonicalText: Other pupils mocked her spelling and the things she had never been taught. The school's history describes her anger and shame. She remembered the humiliation.
arc.sourceNote: Source-led vignette, not recreated scenes. The 1886 speech is a contemporary document; school feelings and disciplinary history are retrospective accounts. No full-moment or publication approval is asserted.

arc.canonicalText: She learned to read and advanced in her studies. Later, she remembered a weekly poetry class as the part of school that absorbed her. The plays stayed with her.
arc.sourceNote: Source-led vignette, not recreated scenes. The 1886 speech is a contemporary document; school feelings and disciplinary history are retrospective accounts. No full-moment or publication approval is asserted.

arc.canonicalText: Doing well in lessons did not end her trouble with the school's rules. She came close to being expelled more than once. Staff who knew her intervened.
arc.sourceNote: Source-led vignette, not recreated scenes. The 1886 speech is a contemporary document; school feelings and disciplinary history are retrospective accounts. No full-moment or publication approval is asserted.

arc.canonicalText: Nearly six years after arriving, she gave the address at her class's graduation. She thanked the people who had supported their education. She was twenty.
arc.sourceNote: Source-led vignette, not recreated scenes. The 1886 speech is a contemporary document; school feelings and disciplinary history are retrospective accounts. No full-moment or publication approval is asserted.

arc.canonicalText: In that address, she said the search for knowledge would continue after school. The school's history records a less certain prospect alongside those words. She feared having to return to the almshouse. Her next work was unclear.
arc.sourceNote: Source-led vignette, not recreated scenes. The 1886 speech is a contemporary document; school feelings and disciplinary history are retrospective accounts. No full-moment or publication approval is asserted.

arc.canonicalText:
Her name was Anne Sullivan.

She became Helen Keller's teacher.

Your life is not theirs. But a piece of this story may still sit beside you.

You do not have to know what comes after this. You are allowed to need time.

dramatizationLimits: Seven schema roles retain reader compatibility; this deliberately short source-led vignette does not claim full scene or 700–950-word compliance.
No invented classroom, first lesson, graduation gesture, direct dialogue or private motive.
The address is contemporary; remembered school experience and later institutional history cannot establish every private feeling or exact day.
No implication that neglect or impairment was necessary, or graduation guaranteed work.
avoidRules: Do not turn institutional neglect into a necessary gift.
Do not move the 1887 Keller teaching episode into this stage.
Do not treat partial sight improvement as the sole explanation for learning.
Do not claim the valedictory address erased anxiety about employment.
